The police in Berlin formally stop investigating small crime (Translation in the comments)

Berlin - The decision of Klaus Kandt, the president of the police in Berlin, to stop investigating minor crime sparked a controversy within the police force. The Berliner Zeitung (Engl. "Berlin's Newspaper") reported last week about the decision of the police president to only investigate cases of pickpocketing when there are good chances of success. The corresponding order was already issued last year. Back then it referred not to pickpocketing but to bicycle theft.

Increased number of cases

Now the order also applies for pickpocketing. The number of cases has continuously been increasing since 2009. Last year the police registered 40,400 cases. This is an increase of almost 8300 cases compared to the year before. The prosecution rate, however, stayed unchanging low at about 4%. In light of these numbers, it only makes sense to open an investigation when there is a good chance of success, informs the leader of the police.

The Association of German Criminal Investigators (BDK) has a different opinion about the matter. "It doesn't make sense to investigate, when there is nothing to investigate. The question is, however, who is making this decision and if there is enough qualified personnel to pursue the investigation", says the state president of the BDK, Michael Böhl.

Serial crime isn't always immediately recognized, say the investigators. You need years of experience. Organized theft bands often travel from East Europe to Berlin. They always travel using the same routes and contacts in the city, before they start the theft tour.

The detectives must know who these contacts are, and they must also be acquainted with the internal workings of the clans. We have been successful in the past, because the files of these small crime stayed open.

"If a detective knows that an apparently innocent case will be closed immediately, then the required qualitative examination becomes unimportant". The police union thinks the goal of this order is to reduce the piles of files. This makes the politicians rejoice and allows the police to save money. The hope of getting more human resources continues to disappear.

Bodo Pfalzgraf, state president of the German Police Union (DPoLG) also says: "It is possible that by not investigating a simple case, we overlook cases of serial crime". According to the law regarding criminal investigation there is no such thing as small crime. "Each reported crime has the right to be investigated", so the president of the union. However, there should be some time constraints for such investigations.

The attorneys stay calm

For him it's pretty clear that with this order the scope of the police work will be reduced without having to hire more personnel. Federal attorneys are calm. When there is no more possibilities to successfully prosecute someone, when everything possible has been done, then the case is closed. But then he adds, that judgment to decide it is different for each of his colleagues. "We also lack personnel. The pressure is huge", explains the lawyer.

The investigators see the new order as the legalization of crime at the victim's cost.

Oddly enough studies in the 90s proved that when you let small crimes slip (graffiti, vandalism, pick-pocketing) you create a sense of lawlessness that invites both greater criminality from established criminals, new small-criminality from previous would-be-criminals and a sense of apathy and abandon from the public, especially the victims.

They proved the studies correct (at least in one instance) when the national railway service kept on replacing bad furniture for a period of a year or so after each case of vandalism, resulting in a huge drop of bad behaviour on trains.

Obviously Berlin cops would need a capacity-increase to go after both the 'new' migrant criminality of rapes, murders and thefts and the small time crime, but maybe that is where (in a sane society) Soldiers of Odin-type groups and neighbourhood watches could come in.
